the-tragical-history-of-doctor-faustus-f: Christopher Marlowe's great tragedy in its 1604 first printing: the scholar Faustus sells his soul to the devil for twenty-four years of power and pleasure. The most famous bargain in English literature, told in mighty blank verse. This quarto preserves the play in its earliest form, before later editors tidied it up.
king-henry-iv-part-1-pg1516: Prince Hal's double life drives this edition of Shakespeare's richest history play: by night he roisters with the fat rogue Falstaff, by day he readies for the rebellion marching on Shrewsbury. Tavern laughter one scene, battlefield honor the next. Comedy and kingship in perfect, thrilling balance.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum: Volume sixteen: the Silesian Wars, and Maria Theresa's doomed struggle to recover her stolen province. Carlyle narrates campaigns with a soldier's eye and a prophet's voice. The making of Prussia as a great power, told at immense length. For the historically hardy.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-16: Volume sixteen carries the memoir toward its final pages. Bourrienne ties up loose ends and gives his last judgments on the great drama. The secretary who saw it all has the final word here. An essential close to a firsthand history.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-16: The sixteenth volume finds Montaigne in a mellow mood. He writes of conversation, solitude, and the quiet pleasures of the mind. The essays feel like evening talk with an old friend. Gentle wisdom from the tower study.
plos-pone-0357916:
Van-Minh Nguyen and three colleagues ask whether a preliminary weld can save additively manufactured shafts from early fatigue death, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their hollow shafts are built by wire arc printing steel onto stacked rings. The print alone left a hairline unfused seam at each ring joint. Cyclic bending would find that seam. A designed experiment varied current, bead overlap, speed, and ring thickness over thirty runs to optimize the joined version.

The optimized pre joined shafts lasted about half again as long in rotating bending tests as print only shafts, roughly four hundred ninety thousand cycles against three hundred twenty-seven thousand. Scatter between specimens also narrowed. Microscopy explained the gain: the pre weld fused the ring wall completely, while the print only seam gaped slightly at the bore. The authors flag the small sample size, but the mechanism and the margin point the same way.
plos-pone-0356816:
Nari Kim leads a team of eight giving veterinarians a ruler for bear hearts, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Heart disease is common in captive bears, but judging heart size on an X-ray needs a species specific reference. The method measures the heart against the spine's vertebrae. The team reviewed chest radiographs from forty-six healthy sanctuary bears, twenty-two Asiatic black bears and twenty-four sun bears, measuring the scale on two views and recording chest shape.

Both species centered near ten and two thirds vertebrae on the side view. The chest on the front view read slightly higher, especially in sun bears. The two species' heart scores did not differ significantly, though their chests did: black bears run deeper relative to width. Sex, age, weight, and condition showed no significant pull on the score. Sanctuary vets now have numbers to judge enlargement by, instead of guessing.
plos-pone-0357816:
Debela Abdeta Efa, Megersa Akasa, and Yobsan Tamiru published a 2026 survey in PLOS ONE of parasites infecting fish in Lake Hawassa, Ethiopia. The lake supports a local fishing economy, yet its fish parasites had barely been documented. Over the 2023–2024 season the team examined three farmed and wild species, tilapia, catfish, and a local barb, checking skin, gills, and internal organs and recording each fish's size, sex, and weight.

Nearly nine in ten fish carried at least one parasite, and the team collected well over a thousand individual parasites in total. The haul spanned worm groups, single-celled parasites, small crustaceans, and leeches. Infection levels varied with the fish's sex, weight, and length. Because some of these parasites damage fish health and market value, the survey gives local fishery managers a first baseline for monitoring the lake's stocks.
plos-pone-0357116:
Lee Rooney, Gerard McMahon, and Rodney Kennedy published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on a small equipment question with practical consequences: where on the back should athletes wear a GPS tracker? Manufacturers recommend the upper back, between the shoulder blades, but units often slip. The team fitted players with two units at once, upper and mid-back, comparing both against measured ground truth during a team-sport circuit and sprint tests.

The upper-back unit matched the truth closely, with tiny bias for distance and low variability, and strong agreement for peak speed. The mid-back unit badly underestimated distance, varied more, and the two placements could not be treated as interchangeable for distance at all. A shift of only a hand's width down the back was enough to spoil the numbers. Teams, they advise, should enforce the recommended placement, because load decisions built on slipped sensors rest on sand.
plos-pone-0343416:
Lisa J. Wallis and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE on the welfare fallout of importing rescue dogs into the United Kingdom, a trade that has grown sharply. The title quotes a stakeholder's verdict that the practice sometimes just shifts a problem. The team interviewed and ran focus groups with over fifty people across the system, rescuers, transporters, trainers, vets, officials, fosterers, and owners, and read online forum threads too.

Seven themes emerged, covering dogs unfit to travel, transport welfare, infectious disease, and owner novelty, plus regulation and enforcement. New owners often met a dog unlike the one described, with costly health or behavior surprises, and some dogs were mismatched to their households. Rescue groups were seen as owing honest information and support around adoption, delivered inconsistently. Cross-border movement was hard to police, with gaps in compliance, resources, and communication between sectors.
plos-pone-0352116:
Pan Gu and a team of psychologists ask how well people judge where another person is looking, and how that skill shifts with mental health traits. Reading gaze is a basic social skill that often falters in conditions marked by social trouble. In their 2026 study, just over one hundred adults viewed faces online with varied gaze angles, head turns, and added visual noise, and said whether each face seemed to look at them.

Noisier images and mismatched head and eye directions made judgments less exact and more self-focused for everyone. Higher autism traits linked to lower exactness, while higher social anxiety linked to sharper basic judgments but bigger drops under noise. Gu and colleagues say gaze reading rests on both raw sensing and self-related habits, which split differently across traits.
plos-pone-0356916:
CORRECTION: The PLOS One Editors issued this Correction in 2026 to a plan by Helena Pernice and colleagues. The plan covers a registry study of amyloidosis, a disease where misshapen proteins damage many organs. Care is split across clinics. The registry, based at Berlin's Charité center, is set up to follow patients across clinics in one shared record. Nerve, heart, and blood clinics are among them.

The fix is paperwork only. The author workplace listings printed with the plan were wrong. The notice reprints the full, correct list for all authors. It spans the amyloidosis center and its partner units. No methods, aims, or data change. Readers citing the plan should take author addresses and credits from the corrected version.
plos-pone-0353216:
Yuan Zhao and colleagues tested how managing emotions affects focused problem solving when the mind is already loaded. Convergent thinking, narrowing to one right answer, underpins much study and work. Their 2026 experiment split ninety-three undergraduates into three groups: reframing feelings, suppressing their expression, or simply watching.

Everyone solved word-association puzzles under high and low mental load. Scores were higher under low load for all groups, and strategy made no clear difference to scores. Speed told another story. Under heavy load, reframing produced faster answers than free watching. Under light load, suppression was fastest. Zhao and colleagues say the best emotion strategy may depend on how busy the mind already is.
plos-pone-0355216:
Florian Vogt and colleagues try in 2026 to build a simple symptom rule for spotting chikungunya fever at basic clinics in Kinshasa, Congo. The mosquito borne illness looks like many other fevers in the region, and lab tests are scarce. Patients with suspected infection during an outbreak gave clinical details and blood for virus and antibody tests, plus a malaria check.

About two in five truly had acute infection. Pain in knees and shoulders showed some signal, but both a tree based rule and a regression model missed most cases or mislabelled many. The authors conclude that symptoms alone cannot guide care here and better test access is essential.
plos-pone-0355416:
Bo Gong and co-authors reanalyse a large surgical database in 2026. The patients were adults who had brain tumour surgery. The team asked one main question. Does long term steroid use before surgery raise clot risk? The clot of interest forms in the lungs after surgery. A blood cell ratio was tested as a link in the chain.

More than fifteen thousand patients were included in the study. Steroid users got lung clots more often than non users. The link stayed after other factors were counted. Part of the link ran through the blood cell ratio. The authors call for fresh studies to confirm the finding. They also want tests of whether the ratio can guide prevention.
plos-pone-0354816:
Koichi Ohata led a team of eight authors on this 2026 chart review of an antifungal drug, isavuconazole, in Japanese patients with blood cancers. Forty-five patients treated between 2023 and 2025 had their lab values and heart rhythm intervals tracked over time. A subgroup also received a leukemia drug known to stretch the heart's electrical recovery.

Liver enzyme rises were uncommon and passed quickly, and no meaningful lab deterioration appeared. In the subgroup, the antifungal pairing actually showed shorter heart intervals than the leukemia drug alone. Ohata judges the antifungal reassuringly safe in this fragile group.
plos-pone-0352316:
Adooru L N Arunkumar led a team of six authors on this 2026 machining study of milling YXR-7, a hard tool steel used for dies. Twenty-seven experimental runs varied cutting depth, feed, speed, and a nano-particle cutting fluid, measuring surface smoothness, material removed, and tool wear. A fuzzy multi-criteria ranking method then weighed the trade-offs.

One run stood out, pairing a smooth finish and low tool wear with a high removal rate. The authors present their ranking method as a robust way to tune precision machining of hard steels with less waste.
plos-pone-0354916:
Alnazzawi, in a 2026 study, asks whether free-text notes in patient records can help predict heart disease. Heart disease covers problems such as heart failure, heart attack, and stroke, and high blood pressure and diabetes raise the risk. Finding risk signs early in messy clinical notes could help doctors act sooner.

The approach maps words in written records onto structured traits, then feeds those traits into a boosting model that learns from many small decision trees. Training drew on both a corpus of clinical narratives and a classic structured heart disease data set. The model sorted patients by whether heart disease was present with solid accuracy in the low eighties, in percent terms. Alnazzawi presents the method as a way to flag high-risk patients from records that clinics already keep.
plos-pone-0353016:
Handley and colleagues, in a 2026 study, test whether giving birth at a hospital with a higher official level of maternity care protects mothers from severe complications. Guidelines sort hospitals into four levels, from basic to regional centers, so risky births can be steered to the right place. Evidence that the sorting itself helps was thin. The team studied more than three million births in four states.

Severe complications, counted without blood transfusion cases, actually rose with hospital level, which mostly reflects that sicker mothers are sent upward. After adjusting for risk, mothers at the most basic hospitals had slightly lower complication rates than those at top centers overall. Yet among mothers with common, treatable problems such as bleeding or infection, one middle level did worse than top centers. The authors read this as a warning: level labels alone do not guarantee safety.
plos-pone-0329716:
Ru-Gang An and seven colleagues examine delirium after heart surgery in children born with heart defects, in this 2026 PLOS ONE database study. Delirium — sudden confusion and disturbed awareness — is a recognised risk after major surgery, but its scale in these young patients was unclear. Records from a national United States hospital sample covering 2010 to 2019 held more than one hundred and eighty-seven thousand such operations.

About two children in every hundred were diagnosed with delirium afterwards. Those children carried more other illnesses, stayed longer, cost more, and died in hospital more often. Clotting disorders, fluid and salt imbalances, and pre-existing paralysis predicted it. Spotting high-risk children early could focus preventive care where it counts.
plos-pone-0342616:
Bethsabe Romero and Amanda Burbage mine national survey data to profile first-generation medical school applicants in the United States, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. These applicants — the first in their families to attend college — covered applications from 2017 to 2024, totalling over a quarter of a million people. About one applicant in eight was first-generation, and all who reported family finances came from low-income backgrounds.

Their motives leaned toward security, escaping career debt, and social change. Yet their acceptance rate lagged far behind other applicants', as did enrolment, with family obligations and older age among the drags. The authors map exactly where support — money, mentoring, time — would help most.
plos-pone-0339016:
David Calderón Guzmán and seven colleagues test whether plant flavonoids can shield the brain and gut in a rat model of Huntington's disease, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Huntington's involves inflammation and oxidative damage; the model uses a toxin that produces both, layered on a bacterial challenge. Young rats received the toxin alone or with a mixture of three flavonoids, including rutin, while brain chemicals and damage markers were measured in cortex, cerebellum, and gut lining.

The toxin depressed dopamine in the cortex and left visible nerve-cell lesions. With flavonoids aboard, fat-damage markers in the cerebellum fell and several enzyme activities shifted toward normal. The results are early and mixed across brain regions, but they justify asking whether dietary flavonoids can blunt part of Huntington's damage.
plos-pone-0354016:
Chertemps and colleagues mapped the sense genes of deep-sea shrimp in a 2026 study. Four kinds of shrimp live near hot vents on the floor of the Atlantic Ocean, where water swings between scalding and cold and light never reaches. To survive there, the shrimp must smell chemicals and feel heat with great precision.

One vent shrimp carried the largest set of smell-related genes yet found in any shrimp-like animal. Many of those genes belong to one fast-growing family, which hints they help the animal read the mixed chemicals around vents. The team also found many heat-sensing genes, while other sense proteins seemed to serve wider jobs in the body.
plos-pone-0353116:
Xu and colleagues modeled earthquake protection for linked twin towers in a 2026 study. Connecting towers with bridges can worsen shaking, so the team placed special damping layers inside the towers. The layers use lead-core bearings that both isolate and absorb energy, a method meant to avoid the tipping risk of base isolation in tall buildings.

Models with damping on both sides shed more energy and shook less than single-sided designs. Smart placement of layers also limited dangerous bending. Vertical shaking, however, was barely reduced by either design. The work shows promise for sideways quakes while honestly flagging the vertical gap for future research.
plos-pone-0353716:
Sikder and colleagues analyzed early breastfeeding in Bangladesh using a national health survey from 2022 in a 2026 paper. Starting breastfeeding within an hour of birth protects newborns, and mothers reported that timing for nearly five thousand births. About sixty-three in one hundred babies started within the hour.

Skin-to-skin contact right after birth stood out as a strong support for early starting. Rates varied by region and birth setting, with cesarean births a weak point. The authors urge focused help in hospitals and after surgical births. Closing the remaining gap could prevent newborn illness in a country where most births now occur in facilities.
plos-pone-0350516:
Jingyuan Wu and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study teaching language models to spot harmful drug reactions. The clues hide in doctors' free-text notes. The team worked from a national benchmark dataset and a second set from Vanderbilt University Medical Center. They fine-tuned several transformer models. They compared two ways of chopping long notes into pieces the models can digest.

Cutting notes into structured chunks generally beat sliding a fixed word window across them. One long-document model, paired with chunking, gave the most balanced results across both datasets. Chunk size mattered even when notes fit within model limits. Scores fell on the real hospital data compared with the benchmark. The authors report that gap honestly, as they offer practical guidance for building such safety tools.
plos-pone-0351316:
Xiongbao Zhang and seven coauthors link gut germs to stamina in this 2026 study. First they set young adults who train often against peers who sit most of the day. Surveys logged how much each group moved and ate. Stool tests then mapped each group's gut germs. The active group hosted a richer, more varied mix. Helpful kinds, such as Veillonella and Faecalibacterium, thrived there.

Then came the telling test. The team moved gut germs from human donors into mice. Mice given the active donors' germs ran with clearly better stamina. Germs from the sitting donors gave no such boost. The result hints that the germ mix of active people is no bystander. It can itself lift the power to keep going, which opens a path toward germ-based aids for sport and recovery.
plos-pone-0352416:
Amanda Chen, Martha Jeong, and Michele Rigolizzo study how luck distorts learning in this 2026 report. Learners often fail despite good strategies, through bad luck. They also succeed despite poor strategies, through good luck. Both moments could teach something, if read correctly. The authors ask whether people read them correctly. Pilot data hinted at an asymmetry worth chasing.

In the pilot, people assumed noise explained failure more readily than success. They therefore treated success as the more informative signal. The main research tests a sharper worry. An early lucky success may damage learning more than an early unlucky failure. Learners who over-trust a fluky win may stop improving a weak strategy. Those burned by bad luck at least keep searching. The work matters anywhere feedback is noisy, from classrooms to trading floors.
plos-pone-0352016:
Lei Ren and Shixin Jin taught neural networks to solve a class of diffusion equations whose memory strength changes over time. Such equations, used for spread in messy materials where the past lingers, carry a fractional order that itself drifts, and normally both the solution and the order must be guessed separately. Their physics-informed design embeds the equation inside the network's training goal.

Two networks work as a pair: one sketches the spreading solution, the other learns the drifting order from the same data. In tests the pair recovered both with tiny errors, and kept working when the data were noisy or the order changed roughly. Inverse problems of this kind show up in groundwater flow, drug spread, and materials science, so a solver that also reads the hidden order off sparse data has wide use.
plos-pone-0350616:
Eun-Ji Lee and colleagues mined police crash records from Cheongju, a mid-sized South Korean city, to find which factors turn a crash severe. They ran the same data through classical logistic regression and through four machine learning models with explanation tools, trusting only the risk factors both families agreed on. Policy, not prediction alone, was the goal.

Three culprits topped both approaches: running signals, neglecting safe-driving duties, and missing median barriers on undivided roads. Because the methods converge, officials can act with more confidence than a single model would justify. The study is a template as much as a result: pairing an old statistical workhorse with explainable machine learning gives cities findings that are both modern and defensible in a council meeting.
plos-pone-0351216:
Sepsis that starts outside the lungs often spreads damage to them, and magnesium levels in the blood may play a part. Taotao Peng and colleagues mined an American intensive care database covering more than four thousand eight hundred such patients, in this 2026 PLOS One analysis.

Patients who developed lung complications died more often within ninety days. Risk followed a U shape across magnesium levels: both the lowest and highest ranges fared worse, with the highest group worst of all. A middle band looked safest. The authors suggest magnesium deserves monitoring as an early warning sign, while cautioning that records alone cannot prove the mineral itself drives the harm.
plos-pone-0350416:
Arizona changed three rules in 2023 to get more children eating school meals, and Shreya Raval and colleagues tracked what happened across about seventeen hundred public and charter schools. Their 2026 PLOS One study used meal records over time, comparing periods before and after each change.

First the state dropped the small fee charged to lower-income families; participation by those students jumped about ten percent for breakfast and lunch alike. Two federal changes followed, widening automatic eligibility and letting more schools serve everyone free. After all three, participation rose across every group. The authors offer the sequence as evidence that paperwork and small fees, not appetite, were the barriers.
plos-pone-0351416:
Defenders of an accused person sometimes flip the story. They call the accused the real victim. Stephen J Flusberg and colleagues tested how far that move travels. Five experiments involved nearly three thousand people. The study appeared in PLOS One in 2026. Earlier work had shown the effect in one sexual assault setting.

Fictional news stories covered several kinds of assault claims. One story involved a police shooting of an unarmed civilian. Labeling one side the victim shifted support everywhere. Readers who credited the victim language showed the strongest shifts. Gender and politics changed little. The authors warn the tactic works broadly. It is not limited to headline cases.
plos-pone-0349216:
Eman S El-Atfy and colleagues propose a new statistical test for whether waiting times follow the simplest random pattern, called exponential. Many fields, from medicine to machine life, need that check. Their test targets cases where average remaining life shrinks over time. Math built on a classic transform plus paired comparisons gives a test that keeps its scale and settles to a known shape in large samples.

Simulated trials with full and cut off data showed the test beating older checks at spotting the target pattern. Real examples included COVID death data and clinical survival data, where the test found clear departures. A bonus proof shows the logic still holds under a common shock model for failures.
plos-pone-0351116:
Ersan Arslan and colleagues tested how heat strains young soccer players during small training games. Sixteen players, about sixteen years old, played two against two and four against four games in low, moderate, and high heat. Heart rate, distance run, effort ratings, and ear temperature were tracked across repeated bouts in each condition.

Hotter conditions raised heart strain and felt effort step by step in both game sizes. Distance covered and ear temperature did not shift clearly with heat. Bout by bout patterns showed strain built unevenly as games repeated. Coaches should read heat load from heart and effort signals, the authors suggest, not from distance alone, and plan breaks accordingly in warm weather.
plos-pone-0350816:
Ballerina X S Chong and colleagues studied work hours and well being. Data came from a New Zealand panel study. Close to twenty five thousand adults took part. Waves ran from 2020 to 2023. The method mimics a trial on the same people. It shifts hours up or down by ten per week.

Ten extra hours raised fatigue most clearly. Sleep fell too. Ten fewer hours lowered fatigue most clearly. Weight and felt health moved in hoped for ways. Those shifts hinged more on hidden factors. Most of twenty eight outcomes barely moved. Recovery is where long hours bite hardest.
plos-pone-0330816:
Ri Nin and Kazuo Mori tested in 2026 whether old Japanese words for husband and wife still carry sexist weight in the mind. One term literally means master, the other inside the house, yet both are in everyday use.

University students took a paper based test that reveals hidden word associations, comparing the old terms with neutral ones. The old pair showed no stronger male dominant links than the neutral pair, suggesting the words have become plain labels for many speakers. A gap remained, though: men rated male linked terms more warmly, while women did not. Hidden bias, the authors note, can linger in speakers even as words fade.
plos-pone-0349516:
Susana Marquez Rosales and co-authors watched bacteria inside living zebrafish guts in 2026 to see how a meal changes their behaviour. Food shapes gut microbes, but behaviour inside a real intestine is hard to observe, and the see through larvae solve that.

Two gut strains were compared: one that clumps into large groups in unfed fish, and a mobile one that can damage tissue. The team fed larvae rotifers cleaned of most microbes by ultraviolet light, separating the effect of food itself from new germs arriving. Imaging then showed how feeding shifts clumping, movement, and place in the gut.
plos-pone-0350116:
Noemi Cucurachi and co-authors tested live monitoring for a mishap in nuclear medicine in 2026: injected radioactive tracer leaking into tissue instead of the vein. Leaks distort scans and, in therapy, can burn the tissue they pool in.

Portable detectors watched nearly nine hundred diagnostic scans and a small set of therapies. Dozens of leaks were caught live and confirmed on images. Curves of dose over time yielded simple cut-offs that flag a leak, and correction factors linked to curve features. Catching leaks during injection lets staff act at once and fix scan numbers before reading.
plos-pone-0345916:
Rubeena Zakar and co-authors evaluated a year of community based teaching for public health students in Lahore, Pakistan, in 2026. The module aimed at mother and child health, sending undergraduates into a semi-urban community under supervision rather than keeping them in lecture halls.

Knowledge, skills, and practical competence were measured before and after with tests, observed exams, and surveys, while group talks and reflection logs added depth. Scores rose significantly across every mother and child health domain. The design shows community placement as the engine of the gain, a model other schools in similar settings could copy directly.
plos-pone-0344916:
Bingbing Qian and co-authors borrowed the math of disease outbreaks to model how harm spreads through an ecosystem. In their 2026 study, species become nodes in a food web, and a disturbance, such as a pest outbreak, passes along feeding links much like an infection. Species can sit in one of three states: undisturbed, disturbed, or recovered.

The team derived a threshold number that decides the disturbance's fate. Below the threshold, the web settles back to a calm state, while above it the disturbance persists across the system. The threshold depends on the food web's shape, how easily harm spreads, and how fast species recover. Tests on a real New Zealand pine forest web, with eighty-five species, matched the theory. The framework also points to where protection efforts could slow a spreading disturbance.
plos-pone-0349116:
Lauri Rapeli and Kim Backström ran a rare experiment on how to persuade politicians to join a research survey panel. Survey response is falling everywhere, and politicians are an especially reluctant group. Their 2026 study emailed more than seven thousand Finnish local politicians, randomly varying the invitation's appeal: helping others, personal benefit, or advancing science.

None of the three appeals worked better than the others. The authors conclude the altruism-versus-self-interest framing simply does not move politicians, and researchers need different tools to recruit them. Who did volunteer followed a pattern of its own: older politicians, those in urban municipalities, and those on the political left joined at higher rates. The study offers a sobering baseline for anyone surveying elected officials.
plos-pone-0350016:
Abdulsalam Al-Shami and co-authors measured blood ferritin, a marker tied to iron overload, in Yemeni teenagers and young adults with sickle cell anemia treated in Sana'a. Repeated transfusions load these patients with iron, yet ferritin also rises with inflammation, so reading it takes care. Their 2026 study enrolled eighty patients over six months and compared ferritin with blood counts and social factors.

About eighty-five percent of patients had elevated ferritin, with a typical value far above the normal ceiling. Ferritin tracked with white blood cell counts, hinting that inflammation inflates the numbers alongside true iron burden. Red cell measures and social factors showed no clear predictive power. The authors, noting their small sample, urge monitoring that separates iron overload from inflammation before treatment decisions are made.
plos-pone-0348316:
Shoukat Ullah and colleagues built a hybrid computer model that judges products from online customer reviews. Instead of only sorting reviews into positive or negative, their system rates how easy a product seems to use and how well it works. They trained it on Amazon reviews labeled by hand using ideas from appraisal theory.

The model pairs a DistilRoBERTa reader, which grasps the meaning of review text, with a BiGRU network that follows word order. Explainable AI checks showed which words drove each rating. For shoppers and sellers, ratings split into ease of use and effectiveness carry more useful detail than a single sentiment score.
plos-pone-0349016:
Xiaonan Li and Lin Mao surveyed more than eighteen hundred Chinese college students about smartphone habits and sleep problems, then mapped how the symptoms connect to each other. Instead of treating each condition as a single score, they built networks showing which symptoms sit at the center and which ones bridge the two problems. A second method probed which symptoms may drive others.

Standard questionnaires measured phone addiction and sleep quality for every student. Network maps like these can show, for example, whether poor sleep fuels late-night phone use or the reverse. Finding the bridge symptoms matters because treating a bridge may loosen both problems at once. The authors also compared the networks of men and women for differences.
plos-pone-0335116:
Stephen Mensah Arhin and colleagues surveyed more than two thousand doctors, nurses, and pharmacists across Ghana about medication errors and their reporting. Errors in prescribing and giving medicines cause preventable harm worldwide, and reporting systems in poorer countries are often patchy. The survey measured what professionals know about error types, what they actually do, and whether they know reporting channels exist.

Recognition was strongest for wrong-dose and wrong-patient errors, at over four in five respondents, but knowledge thinned for other categories, and awareness of reporting systems varied. Finding the exact gaps matters because a reporting system nobody knows about or trusts cannot catch mistakes. The multicenter snapshot gives Ghanaian health leaders a map for safety training.
plos-pone-0348016:
Hamad Al-Ibrahim, Arokiasamy Perianayagam, and Noor Al Thani made a new scale to gauge how people in Qatar think about buying things. Qatar is rich, mixed, and changing fast. More than two thousand people, both Qataris and those who moved there, filled out a long form on buying, rank, thrift, and care for the earth.

Four clear themes came out: love of goods as a mark of rank, wasteful splurging, thrift, and care for the earth. Checks showed the scale reads the same for locals and newcomers, men and women, rich and poor, so group scores can be compared with trust. Fast growth sets goods and green aims at odds, and this tool can track that strain.
plos-pone-0348216:
Ariel Zeleznikow-Johnston, Emil Kendziorra, and Andrew McKenzie surveyed three hundred thirty-four American physicians about preserving the dead for possible future revival, through freezing or chemical fixation. The October 2025 poll ran on a verified physician platform. It asked how likely good preservation is to keep enough brain information for revival. It also asked what doctors think about helping procedures and the ethics around them.

The median doctor put the chance at about one in four under ideal conditions, and roughly twenty-eight percent found revival at least somewhat plausible. Views on steps like giving blood thinners before death, and on whether offering preservation fits patient-centered care, were also mapped. The results give the first broad read of medical opinion on a practice usually debated without data.
plos-pone-0348516:
Emmanuela Anele and colleagues surveyed clawed frogs and their worm parasites across Nigeria's ecological zones, identifying both hosts and parasites by shape and by DNA. Five frog species were found, one of them thriving across four different savanna zones. The frogs carried thirteen worm species from roundworm and flatworm lineages.

Roundworms proved the generalists, infecting several frog species across wide areas, while the flatworms were pickier about hosts, and every parasite specialized on a particular organ or a matching pair of organs. Frogs sit at the junction of water and land food webs, so their parasite communities read out ecosystem health. A mapped baseline for Nigeria lets later surveys detect ecological change through what lives inside the frogs.
plos-pone-0349416:
Yuki Yonekura and colleagues asked whether heavier Japanese adults being treated for diabetes cost the health system more, separating overweight from obesity and men from women. Japan's obesity rates are far below Western levels, so the cost question could not be answered from foreign data. Insurance records and national health checkup data from fiscal 2008 and 2009 were linked for the analysis.

Statistical models compared total, outpatient, and hospital spending across weight groups while adjusting for age, blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar control, and smoking. They also tested the odds of crossing a high annual spending threshold. Diabetes already strains budgets; knowing how much extra weight adds, and for whom, helps insurers and clinics aim prevention where it pays.
plos-pone-0348616:
Jun Chen and colleagues tackled the seams and distortions that appear when drone photographs are stitched into one wide map. Tall buildings lean differently in overlapping shots, defeating many stitching tools or slowing them down. Their method reframes stitching as a pixel-by-pixel choice: for every spot in the overlap, pick which source photo shows it best, guided by a twin network that compares the candidates.

A second trick predicts the choices at low resolution and expands them, since the choices barely change across scales, avoiding retraining and heavy computation. Across four drone image sets the approach beat leading rivals on picture quality by wide margins while cutting processing time by up to nearly nine tenths. The authors pitch it for large mapping jobs where speed and clean joins both matter.
plos-pone-0348816:
Thomas V. Pollet and co-workers re-examine a widely used survey that measures how well new students settle into university life. The survey is usually scored as one single scale. Their 2026 study instead maps how its questions connect to each other, using answers from two hundred forty first-year students at a British university.

The questions grouped into four clusters rather than one. They covered happiness with university life and support, social connection, day-to-day adjustment, and motivation to keep going. The pattern looked much the same for students whose parents had not attended university. Treating the survey as four parts, the authors argue, gives advisers a clearer picture of where a struggling student actually needs help.
plos-pone-0348116:
Bin Chen and colleagues dated rocks that were baked by burning coal seams in China's Junggar Basin, hoping to time when the land was pushed upward and stripped bare. When rising ground brings coal near the surface, it can catch fire on its own, and the scorched rocks record the event. The team measured a helium-based clock in zircon crystals from these burnt rocks.

Three crystals agreed on a main burning episode in the middle Pleistocene, a few hundred thousand years ago, matching a period of uplift around the basin. Two older readings were judged leftovers from before the fire. The study shows burnt coal rocks can serve as rare clocks for recent mountain building.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
One day after Rhodesia's white rulers broke from Britain, the Council condemned the move. On 12 November 1965, it adopted Resolution 216. Ten members voted yes and none voted no. France held back. The minority regime had declared itself free rather than accept majority rule.

The text condemns the break, made by a racist minority. It calls on all states to refuse the regime any standing. No state should grant it aid of any kind. That refusal, set within a day of the break, fixed world policy toward Rhodesia. It held for fifteen years, until majority-rule Zimbabwe emerged in 1980.

Trieste's fate as a free city under UN guard starts with this act of 1947. On 10 January, the Council adopted Resolution 16. The peace treaty with Italy was then being finished. It carved the port city and its hinterland out of both Italy and Yugoslavia. A Free Territory would stand under direct UN care. An open free port formed part of the design.

The Council records its backing for three treaty texts. They cover the land's first regime, its lasting statute, and the free port. It accepts the duties the treaty lays on it. Naming a governor sat among those duties. The Free Territory never took full shape in the end. Trieste was split between Italy and Yugoslavia in 1954.

Tunisia ended its time as a French protectorate in March 1956. Independence brought an application to join the United Nations. The paperwork reached the Council as document S/3622. Resolution 116 was adopted unanimously on 26 July 1956. It was the second meeting in two days on North African admissions, following Morocco's case.

The Council recommended that the General Assembly admit Tunisia. The Assembly welcomed it that November. Tunisia took its seat during a season of rapid decolonization. Its first UN years made it a bridge between the Arab world and the West. This brief resolution records the formal recommendation that opened the door.

A grab of Arab troops on Lebanese soil lit this 1972 clash. Israeli men had seized Syrian and Lebanese staff on 21 June. Cross-border raids had run for years by then. Truce staff sent sheaves of fresh word. Resolution 316 passed on 26 June 1972 by thirteen votes to none. Panama and the United States held back.

Israel was told to heed the whole chain of past texts. All raids on Lebanon had to cease. The Council damned the fresh strikes by name. It voiced grief at deaths from raids and counter-raids alike. One sharp wish stood out: the seized men must be freed, and fast. If they were not, or if Israel balked, the Council would meet at once to weigh next steps. The words had a hard edge rare for the day.

Resolution 1316, adopted on 23 August 2000, deals with a peacekeeping mission that cannot get onto the ground. MONUC, the UN mission for Congo, had been authorized to grow, but poor access, weak security, and limited cooperation from the parties kept it below strength. Two August summits of the Lusaka ceasefire parties had just been held.

The Council extended MONUC's mandate briefly, into October 2000, while it worked with the ceasefire parties and potential troop contributors to create conditions for fuller deployment. It reaffirmed support for the Lusaka agreement and thanked states that had offered troops. Congo's government was called on in particular to remove the obstacles blocking the mission's work.

Sea piracy off Somalia meets a new legal tool in Resolution 1816, passed on 2 June 2008. Pirate raids put food aid for Somalia at risk. They also scared off trade ships and made sea lanes unsafe. World sea reports had charted the raids since 2005. The Council based its reply on the law of the sea pact. It also had the nod of Somalia's own interim rulers.

For six months, states that worked with those rulers could enter Somalia's own waters. They could use all needed force to crush piracy and armed theft at sea, as on the high seas. The grant was fenced with care. It held for Somalia's coast alone, and set no rule for any other shore.

Resolution 416, adopted on 21 October 1977, concerns the United Nations Emergency Force in the Middle East. The force had been set up after the 1973 war to keep Egypt and Israel apart while a wider peace was sought. The Secretary-General reported on the force and warned that letting the search for a full settlement fade could be dangerous.

The Council calls on all parties to carry out Resolution 338, the 1973 call for a ceasefire and peace talks, without delay. It renews the Emergency Force mandate for one more year, until 24 October 1978. It also asks the Secretary-General to report at the end of that year on events in the area and on steps taken toward the settlement the Council wanted.

Fresh tension in Georgia's Kodori Valley shapes Resolution 1716, adopted on 13 October 2006. A Georgian special operation in the upper valley that July had raised Abkhaz fears and breached the 1994 Moscow ceasefire deal. Joint patrols by the UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, and the CIS peacekeeping force had just resumed there.

The Council extends UNOMIG until 15 April 2007. It voices concern at Georgia's moves in the Kodori Valley and urges Tbilisi to keep the valley in line with the Moscow agreement, with no unauthorized troops present. It urges the Abkhaz leadership to take the return of displaced people seriously and to reassure residents of the Gali district about their rights. Both sides are pressed to finish draft papers on non-use of violence and refugee return and to restart talks at the highest level.

Weapon flows into Somalia and Eritrea are targeted by Resolution 1916, adopted on 19 March 2010. The Monitoring Group's March 2010 report documented embargo violations, and the Group itself faced intimidation. Eritrea had been placed under its own arms embargo and sanctions by Resolution 1907 (2009). The Djibouti peace process remained the Council's path for Somalia.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the Monitoring Group for 12 months, adding three experts so it can cover both embargoes. The Group must trace the money and transport routes behind violations, keep draft lists of violators for both countries, brief the Sanctions Committee monthly, and report finally before its mandate ends. For 12 months, the asset freeze does not block funds needed for urgent humanitarian aid in Somalia, with reviews every 120 days. All states, Eritrea included, must cooperate with the Group and guarantee its safety and access.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: On 13 February 1946, at the thirty-first plenary meeting, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 16. It is an election record. The Assembly named the ten members of the new Committee on Contributions. It set four of them to serve two-year terms. It pointed the committee to the Preparatory Commission's guidance on money matters. It asked the committee to bring a detailed plan for sharing United Nations costs. The plan was for the second part of the first session.

General Assembly resolution 69/16 was adopted on 18 November 2014. It adopts the programme of activities for the International Decade for People of African Descent. The Decade runs from 1 January 2015 to 31 December 2024. Its theme is 'recognition, justice and development.' The annexed programme, built on the Durban Declaration and Programme of Action, is the resolution's real substance.

The programme asks states to remove legal and practical obstacles to equality. It asks them to strengthen anti-discrimination law. It asks them to widen access to education, health, housing, and justice for people of African descent. All this is in full consultation with them. The Assembly appoints the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights as coordinator of the Decade. It requests annual progress reports and regular budget funding. It plans a midterm review and a final high-level assessment. The Decade gave the fight against racism a ten-year, program-shaped framework.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force, UNFICYP, is extended on 13 June 2002, to 15 December 2002. The island's government agreed the force was still needed. The Secretary-General's report had also urged urgent work on the humanitarian issue of missing persons from the island's conflict.

The mandate is renewed and a report is due by 1 December 2002. The Turkish Cypriot side and Turkish forces are urged to lift restrictions placed on UNFICYP in June 2000. The military position at Strovilia is to return to what it had been before those restrictions. The force's long watch over the island's ceasefire lines thus continues.

Bomb attacks in Istanbul, Turkey, on 15 and 20 November 2003 are condemned in this text of 20 November. The two rounds of blasts killed and injured many people within one week. Other terrorist acts in various countries are cited in the same statement.

Deepest sympathy goes to the people and governments of Turkey and the United Kingdom and to the victims and their families. All states are urged, as resolution 1373 requires, to cooperate in finding and bringing to justice those who carried out, organized, and sponsored the attacks. The text closes by restating a strengthened resolve to fight terrorism in all its forms.

Weapons still flowed to militias in Ituri and the Kivus, and on 29 July 2005 the arms embargo and related measures on armed groups in eastern Congo are renewed. The ban had been set in 2003 and widened in April 2005. The arms trade is linked to the illegal exploitation of Congo's natural resources.

The parties had again failed to meet the Council's demands, so the embargo measures are renewed for a further period. The group of experts that tracks violations is re-established, and the plan to enforce penalties against people and bodies breaking the ban is restated. States and the Congolese government are pressed to cooperate with the experts and the sanctions committee.

Libya's civil war had just ended when the Council adopted Resolution 2016 on 27 October 2011. Four days earlier, the National Transitional Council had declared the country liberated. The resolution closes the military chapter of the international intervention in Libya.

The Council ended the main powers granted by Resolution 1973 earlier that year. That text had allowed member states to protect civilians and enforce a no-fly zone over Libya. Those powers, and the related ban on flights, would end at the close of 31 October 2011, Libyan time. The Council welcomed the change of power. It urged Libya's new authorities to stop revenge attacks and arrests without legal basis. It also looked ahead to a government that included all parts of society.
un-sc-res-216:
Southern Rhodesia's white minority government declared independence from Britain on its own on 11 November 1965. The Council answered the very next day. Resolution 216, adopted on 12 November 1965, is short, with only two decisions. Both of them are firm.

The Council condemned the unilateral declaration of independence. The declaration had been made by a racist minority, and the regime it created was illegal. All states were called on not to recognize that regime. They also had to refrain from giving it any assistance at all. The text was the Council's first word on Rhodesia's breakaway. Stronger measures, including the sanctions of later years, all built on this refusal to accept the minority regime as lawful.
un-sc-res-316:
Israeli raids into Lebanon brought a sharp rebuke in June 1972. Israeli forces had seized Syrian and Lebanese personnel on Lebanese soil on 21 June. On 26 June 1972 the Council condemned the repeated attacks. It deplored all acts of violence in the exchange. The attacks, it said, broke the Charter and Israel's duties under it. Truce reports covering April to June fed the debate.

Israel had to obey past resolutions and stop all military acts against Lebanon. The Council voiced a strong desire for the captives' quick release. If they were not freed, or if Israel defied the text, the Council would meet again fast. Panama and the United States abstained in the vote.
un-sc-res-1316:
The Congo mission received a short technical extension on 23 August 2000. The Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement was in place, and summits of the Southern African Development Community and of the cease-fire parties had met in August. Yet poor access, weak security, and low cooperation kept the United Nations mission, MONUC, from deploying to its authorized strength. The Secretary-General had written to the Council on 14 August.

The Council extended MONUC's mandate to 15 October 2000. It stressed that this was a technical extension, not a change of course. The government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the other parties were called to lift every obstacle to the mission's deployment and work. All parties bore duty for the safety of United Nations and linked staff across the country. The Secretary-General had to report by 21 September 2000. The Council praised the mission's staff for strong work in hard conditions.
un-sc-res-1816:
Piracy off Somalia met a naval answer on 2 June 2008. Pirate attacks and armed robbery at sea threatened aid deliveries to Somalia and the safety of trade routes. Maritime reports since 2005 showed the attacks going on. Somalia's transitional government lacked the means to stop pirates or to patrol its own waters. The Law of the Sea Convention supplied the legal frame.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council condemned all piracy and armed robbery against ships off Somalia. For six months, states working with the transitional government, and named by it in advance to the Secretary-General, could enter Somalia's territorial waters. They could use all necessary means to repress piracy, in line with the law for the high seas. States were urged to share information, help crews, and bring suspects to trial. The step opened the door to the foreign naval patrols that followed off the Horn of Africa.
un-sc-res-416:
The Sinai emergency force was renewed for a full year on 21 October 1977. The Secretary-General's report on the United Nations Emergency Force guided the Council. He warned that letting the search for a full settlement relax could prove dangerous. He advised one more year for the force. The force had stood between Egypt and Israel since the 1973 war.

The Council called on all parties to carry out resolution 338 (1973) at once. It renewed the Emergency Force's mandate for one year, until 24 October 1978. The Secretary-General had to report at the end of the period on events and on the steps taken toward resolution 338. That text demanded a cease-fire and talks for a just and durable peace. The Council voiced its confidence that the force would be kept with the greatest efficiency and economy.
un-sc-res-1716:
Georgia and its breakaway region of Abkhazia are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1716. The Council adopted it on 13 October 2006. A Georgian move into the upper Kodori Valley that July had raised tensions and strained the 1994 cease-fire.

The text extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, called UNOMIG, until 15 April 2007. It urges Georgia to keep the Kodori Valley in line with the cease-fire deal. It urges Abkhaz leaders to let displaced people return home with safety and dignity. Both sides are pressed to sign papers on no violence and on refugee returns.
un-sc-res-1916:
Somalia and Eritrea are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1916, adopted on 19 March 2010. Weapons kept flowing to both countries in breach of the arms embargoes. Armed groups also stole or misused aid meant for hungry people. The monitors doing this work faced threats and interference.

The text extends the Monitoring Group for twelve months and adds three experts. The group will track money, ships, and routes used to break the embargoes. It will also draft lists of offenders for possible future action. For one year, the asset freeze will not block funds needed to deliver urgent aid in Somalia. The aid coordinator must report every 120 days on how that carve-out works.
europmc-pmc10154216:
Dejanovic and co-workers show that astrocytes and microglia remove synapses in Alzheimer's mouse models through a complement protein, in a 2022 study. Synapses are the contact points where nerve cells pass signals. Their loss tracks closely with memory decline in Alzheimer's disease.

Using combined molecular analyses, the team found that a protein called C1q drives the removal of both excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Brain support cells carried out the pruning as the mice aged. The work points to a shared mechanism behind synapse loss. It also names a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc10623016:
Sender and co-authors counted every immune cell in the human body in 2023. No full census of this kind had been pulled into one view. The team pooled past measures of cell counts by tissue and type. Their aim was a single tally of number, mass, and spread.

An average body holds about 1.8 trillion immune cells, Sender reports. Their total mass comes to roughly 1.2 kilograms. Lymphocytes, a key defence type, make up 40% of the cell count but just 15% of the mass. Neutrophils hold like shares of both. Macrophages are 10% of cells yet near half the mass, due to their large size. The census gives model builders a firm base.
europmc-pmc11006616:
Jamali and co-authors built an AI tool that reads frozen microscope maps of proteins on its own in this 2024 paper. Cryo-EM is a method that images flash-frozen samples to reveal protein shapes. Turning those maps into atom-level models takes expert labour by hand. The team asked whether a neural network could do the job as well.

Their tool, ModelAngelo, fuses the map with protein sequence and shape data in one network. Its protein models matched the quality of expert-built ones, the authors report. For DNA and RNA parts, its backbones matched human accuracy too. When fed unknown proteins, its residue guesses powered database searches that beat human experts at naming the protein. The authors say the tool removes a bottleneck and adds objectivity to the process.
europmc-pmc13191116:
Wong and a very large team released IQ-TREE 3, software for evolutionary trees, in 2026. The tool infers family trees from DNA by maximum likelihood. It is open source and widely used. Version 3 extends version 2 with major features.

New mixture models replace some partitioned model uses. Concordance factors now quantify disagreement between genomic regions. Divergence time estimation is integrated into the package. A full sequence simulator was added for testing methods. Wong keeps the tool current for phylogenomic data at scale. Source code is posted on the project GitHub page. As open source code, it stays free for labs anywhere to use and adapt.
europmc-pmc1323316:
Choi and Pak catalogued biases in health questionnaires in 2005. Survey data drive public health decisions, so accuracy matters. Bias can creep in at design or delivery stages. Their review of the literature sorted every bias type found.

Forty-eight distinct bias types were identified and categorized. Each type comes with an example in the catalogue. Three sources organize the list: question design, whole-form design, and administration. Mechanisms behind each bias are explained in plain terms. Choi supplies a pre-use checklist for spotting bias early. It appeared in Preventing Chronic Disease in 2005.
europmc-pmc1420316:
Brain cells grown in a dish do not sit quiet. Wagenaar and co-authors recorded 58 cultures of rat cortex cells for five weeks in 2006. The cells grew on grids of tiny sensors that pick up their electric spikes. Cultures ranged from sparse to dense.

Dense cultures began firing in bursts sooner than sparse ones. After two weeks, most cultures fired in waves that swept the whole dish. Burst styles varied a great deal, with gaps from one second to five minutes. Some bursts came in tight packs with a set inner shape. Wagenaar shows dish networks stay rich and changeable far longer than past reports claimed.
europmc-pmc1479816:
Drugs that block acetylcholine, a nerve signal, open airways in lung disease. Gosens and co-authors reviewed in 2006 whether the signal does more than tighten airway muscle. In asthma and COPD, airway swelling raises nerve tone and acetylcholine release. The signal also drives mucus output.

Fresh work links the signal to airway wall thickening, a lasting change called remodeling. Many airway cells, not just nerves, make acetylcholine and bear its receptors. Gosens notes one blocking drug slows lung decline in COPD, hinting at wider action. The review argues these drugs may help beyond quick relief of tight airways.
europmc-pmc1481516:
The prostate gland makes huge amounts of citrate, a fruit acid, and stores zinc to do it. Costello and Franklin reviewed in 2006 how that odd chemistry flips in prostate cancer. Healthy gland cells hoard zinc, which blocks citrate burning. Cancer cells lose that hoarding skill.

Without zinc, the cells burn citrate for energy instead. A gene for a zinc intake pump, Zip1, fades in cancer cells. Costello frames zinc as a tumor suppressor, a brake on growth. The review ties lab and clinical proof into one story. It urges more heed to metabolism, long ignored in prostate cancer work.
europmc-pmc1586216:
Evolutionary studies drown in sequence and structure data held apart. Roberts, Eargle, Wright, and Luthey-Schulten built MultiSeq in 2006 to unify them. Public databases then held over 3 million sequences and 35,000 structures.

MultiSeq organizes, aligns, and displays both data kinds for proteins and nucleic acids in one space. It carries standard classifications that users can adjust in an electronic notebook. A new algorithm builds clean evolutionary profiles for families of distant kin, stripping redundancy from alignments. Roberts frames the tool around evolution, but built it flexible enough for other patterns of use.
europmc-pmc1592316:
Leaf pores close when a drought hormone sounds the alarm. Mori and co-authors traced that signal in 2006 to two calcium-sensing proteins in Arabidopsis guard cells, the cells that work the pores. The hormone, abscisic acid, was thought to use calcium, but the sensors were unproven.

Plants missing the two kinases, CPK3 and CPK6, showed impaired channel responses. The hormone could no longer open calcium channels or fully trigger anion channels. Stomata closed only partly. Fast anion channels still worked, hinting at a branched signal path. Mori offers genetic proof that these sensors relay the calcium message.
europmc-pmc1693916:
Plant oils can kill germs, and cinnamon oil leads the pack. Prabuseenivasan, Jayakumar, and Ignacimuthu screened 21 oils in 2006 against six bacterial species, four Gram-negative and two Gram-positive kinds, at four dilutions.

Nineteen oils beat at least one strain. Strong effects came from cinnamon and clove oils, and also from geranium, lemon, lime, orange, and rosemary. Cinnamon worked even at low strength. Aniseed, eucalyptus, and camphor oils were weakest. One soil germ was the most sensitive; a lung germ was the least. The team names cinnamon, clove, and lime oils as broad agents hitting both germ classes.
europmc-pmc1779816: Modeling the worldwide spread of pandemic influenza: baseline case and containment interventions. — a 2005 science paper modeling pandemic flu spread. It models the flu spread for labs. The paper is the flu-model study: the notes on flu spread, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc1971116: Distinct roles for intra- and extracellular siderophores during Aspergillus fumigatus infection. — a 2005 science paper on iron-grabbing germ tools. It maps the siderophore roles. The paper is the siderophore study: the findings on Aspergillus, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2294116: Continuous growth reference from 24th week of gestation to 24 months by gender. — a 2005 science paper on baby growth charts. It builds the growth reference. The paper is the growth-chart study: the findings on babies, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2323616: Discovering sequence motifs with arbitrary insertions and deletions. — a 2008 science paper on finding sequence motifs. It discovers the motif patterns. The paper is the motif study: the findings on sequences, filed here in full session today twice over.
europmc-pmc2361216: E-cadherin transcriptional downregulation by promoter methylation but not mutation is related t — a 2008 science paper on cell-glue gene silencing. It finds the silencing switch for labs. The paper is the switch study: the notes on cell-glue ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2361716: The BOADICEA model of genetic susceptibility to breast and ovarian cancers: updates and extensi — a 2008 science paper on the BOADICEA risk model. It updates the BOADICEA model. The paper is the BOADICEA guide: the findings on the risk model, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2409316: The TOBY Study. Whole body hypothermia for the treatment of perinatal asphyxial encephalopathy: — a 2008 science paper on cooling newborns. It trials the whole-body cooling. The paper is the cooling study: the findings on newborn ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2430616: Alternative-NHEJ is a mechanistically distinct pathway of mammalian chromosome break repair. — a 2008 science paper on alt-NHEJ repair. It defines the distinct pathway. The paper is the pathway study: the findings on chromosome ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2621116: Metabolic engineering of Saccharomyces cerevisiae for the production of n-butanol. — a 2008 science paper on yeast fuel-making. It engineers the yeast fuel for labs. The paper is the fuel study: the notes on yeast ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2635016: Critical Loss of the Balance between Th17 and T Regulatory Cell Populations in Pathogenic SIV I — a 2008 science paper on Th17/Treg imbalance. It finds the critical loss. The paper is the loss study: the findings on SIV ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2697316: The functional role of the inferior parietal lobe in the dorsal and ventral stream dichotomy. — a 2008 science paper on the parietal lobe. It studies the functional dichotomy. The paper is the lobe study: the findings on brain ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2725916: Worldwide emergence of extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis. — a 2008 science paper on extensively drug-resistant TB. It emerges the worldwide TB. The paper is the TB study: the findings on tuberculosis ills, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc2761916: Evaluation of putative reference genes for gene expression normalization in soybean by quantita — a 2008 science paper on soy gene yardsticks. It tests the soy yardsticks for labs. The paper is the yardstick study: the notes on soy ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2765616: Expression profile of MicroRNAs in young stroke patients. — a 2008 science paper on microRNA stroke profiles. It profiles the young-stroke expression. The paper is the profile study: the findings on stroke ills, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2780416: Maize inbreds exhibit high levels of copy number variation (CNV) and presence/absence variation — a 2008 science paper on maize copy-number variation. It exhibits the high levels. The paper is the variation study: the findings on maize ills, filed here in session.
cotta-triall-of-witch-craft-english-1616:
John Cotta, a doctor of Northampton, published The Triall of Witch-craft in 1616. Rather than defend the accused, Cotta attacks the tests used to find witches. His method is a physician's skepticism, turned on the whole business of witch-finding in Jacobean England.

Swimming a suspect, hunting for devil's marks, and watching for familiars all fail his scrutiny. Such proofs, he argues, can brand the innocent as surely as the guilty. Cotta accepts that witchcraft exists, but demands evidence worthy of a court. His book is medicine enlisted against superstition. Doctors would cite it whenever weak tests sent neighbors to the gallows.
roberts-treatise-of-witchcraft-english-1:
Alexander Roberts, a minister, published his Treatise of Witchcraft in 1616, the same year as Cotta's skeptical Triall. Roberts takes the other road. His treatise lays down propositions on witchcraft, point by careful point, building an orderly rulebook for Jacobean readers.

Scripture anchors each proposition, and English cases fill out the doctrine. Roberts writes for the parish pulpit, clear and systematic. His book was meant to be preached from on Sundays.
