arxiv-2606-16516: FPGAs are efficient AI chips, but their memory is tiny — so neural network weights must be stored cleverly. This paper proposes "delta-aware training": training networks so that only the changes (deltas) between weights need storing, shrinking the footprint for resource-constrained FPGAs. It targets hardware-AI engineers.
arxiv-2606-16816: Splitting goods fairly means no one envies another's pile — and with dice in play, 'stochastic dominance' is the fairness bar. This paper checks that bar in time linear in the input: swift checks. It is for fair-split researchers. Swift checks make fair splits real.
22104-the-acorn-planter-a-california-for:
Jack London wrote The Acorn Planter, a California forest play, in 1916, the last year of his life. The stage is a redwood hillside with wide spaces between the great trees. A stream runs from a spring bursting out of the slope. Ferns, brakes, and thickets crowd the forest floor in his opening direction.

London built the play around a Native American planter who sows acorns for a future he will not see. The drama speaks for the redwoods and against waste. It belongs to the Bohemian Grove tradition of outdoor plays written by California authors. Few London works are less known, and few show his love of California land so directly.
arxiv-2601-06816:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Xiangjun Tan and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers axion signal search using hybrid Nuclear–Electronic spin systems. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Conventional nuclear magnetic resonance searches for the galactic axion wind lose sensitivity at low frequencies due to the unfavourable scaling of inductive readout.

Here, the authors propose a hybrid architecture where the hyperfine interaction transduces axion-driven nuclear precession into a high-bandwidth electron-spin readout channel. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07116:
Research by Zi Dong Gao and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with interval [ 𝖵 ⁡ ( s 7 ) , 𝖵 ⁡ ( b. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. We prove that the interval [ 𝖵 , 𝖵 ] [ V. V ] in the lattice of additively idempotent semiring (ai-semiring) varieties has the cardinality of the continuum.

Where S 7 is the smallest nonfinitely based ai-semiring (a three-element algebra). And B 2 1 is the ai-semiring whose multiplicative reduct is the six-element Brandt monoid. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-08516:
Ziqi Ding and co-authors test audio CAPTCHAs against modern audio language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that CAPTCHAs block bots with challenges easy for humans and hard for programs. Audio versions support accessibility alongside visual ones, but their strength is now in doubt.

Large audio language models and speech recognition systems have grown strong enough to threaten audio challenges. How robust current audio CAPTCHAs remain against them was unclear. The team evaluates that robustness and then proposes advances, including audio illusions. Websites need checks that stay accessible to blind users yet resist automated solvers, a balance this work tries to restore.
22313-punch-or-the-london-charivari-volu:
Punch, or the London Charivari, was Britain's famous comic weekly. Volume 150, dated February 2, 1916, comes from the middle of the First World War. Even wartime issues kept the magazine's dry, teasing voice.

One item mocks Austrians and Hungarians quarreling over occupied Serbian land. Each side, Punch notes, ransacks old history for legal arguments. The joke calls the dispute a purely academic question. Learned men, the piece says, love disputing such points. Readers today get wartime London humor at work: sharp about empires and lawyers, yet printed as light weekly fare for the home front.
arxiv-2601-07616:
A short 2026 note treats factories and economies through the lens of thermodynamics, the physics of energy and disorder. Producing goods and services, measured by their value, is framed as creating complexity. That framing lets the author view the production system as an open thermodynamic system. Open systems exchange energy and matter with their surroundings.

From that view, the note builds a simple heuristic model of the production process. Heuristic means a guide for thinking, not an exact law. Models like this try to find limits and patterns that ordinary economics might miss. Readers interested in the physics of economic systems get a compact, speculative treatment. It connects ideas about complexity, value, and energy in a few pages.
arxiv-2601-07716: Raphaël Picard's doctoral thesis studies induced gravitational waves beyond the linear theory used in standard cosmology. Density changes in the early universe can source gravitational waves at higher order, and linear perturbation theory misses part of that process. The thesis was supervised by Karim Malik and David Mulryne at Queen Mary. The record here is mostly front matter and the author's declaration, so this summary names only the topic, author, and supervision it supports.
arxiv-2601-06916:
Mohammed Azeez Khan and co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to train models that guess how atoms pull on each other. Such models are called machine-learned interatomic potentials. To train one, a team must first run costly physics sums for a set of test cases. The paper asks how to pick those cases with care.

The team builds a loop that picks the most useful cases first. Each round, the loop trains on the cases it has, then picks new ones that teach it most. The cases come from two large stores of facts on materials. One store is the Materials Project. The other is the Open Quantum Materials Database. Good picks cut the cost of training while the model stays sharp.
arxiv-2601-08116: Kenneth Gee and Sai Ravela wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how tropical cyclones gain strength. Cyclones are grave hazards, yet past records are small in count and flawed in parts, so direct risk reads are hard to trust. Models fill the gap by faking huge sets of storms, each based on reads of the storm's large-scale setting. The authors fit a stochastic differential equation model of strength gain. They fit it with reanalysis data and with direct reads of real storms.
arxiv-2601-08216:
Zahir Alsulaimawi wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on learning from data split across many sites. In federated learning, each site keeps its own data. The sites sync with a central server again and again as they train. How fast they meet at one model rests on the pace they pick, on how much the data sets differ, and on which sites take part in each round.

Alsulaimawi asks if all those rounds are a must for one task. The task is linear regression in ridge form, a fit with a small curb on the size of its weights. He shows the rounds are not a must. Each site can send a few summary counts, called sufficient statistics, in a single round. The server can then rebuild the exact shared fit from those counts. One round cuts both cost and risk for sites that guard their data, such as clinics and phones.
arxiv-2601-08616: Shuhei Ohyama and Kansei Inamura wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on sets of cluster states in two dimensions plus time. A cluster state is a grid of quantum parts tied as one, used as fuel for quantum computing. The authors build a G-cluster Hamiltonian in 2+1 dimensions and study its traits. The model has a symmetry that joins the group G with a doubled sector. That sector, called 2Rep of G, holds a non-invertible symmetry. It comes from condensing algebra objects in Rep of G.
arxiv-2601-08816:
Weixin Chen and eight co-authors build a pick system that learns from a shared store of past likes. Old pick tools store likes as scores or as dense codes. New agent tools store likes as text notes. But each agent keeps its own notes, so group signs are lost. A song one user loves may guide a pick for a like user.

Their system is called MemRec. It lets agents share a joint note store built from a graph of users and items. The hard part is to pull rich graph facts in with out flooding the agent. The team also needs fast ways to keep the store fresh. A reader who builds picks gets a shared mind plan for agent teams.
arxiv-2601-09316:
Xinming Fang and five co-authors fix MRI scans made from too few samples, by use of a full scan in a next shade. MRI is slow, since it must fill a vast grid of marks. To cut time, staff take few marks and rebuild the rest. A next shade scan, taken in full, can guide that build. Past guides miss where the build errs most, in the rate grid.

Their plan hunts build flaws in the rate form of the scan. It then shifts the sample plan to take more marks where flaws loom. That loop ties scan time to build need. A reader in care scans gets a fast scan plan that spends its marks where they help most.
arxiv-2601-09416:
Yaxi Chen and seven co-authors build an automated way to grade osteosarcoma tissue after chemotherapy. Their 2026 arXiv paper joins radiomics features with deep learning to classify tumor histology. Osteosarcoma is an aggressive bone cancer, and judging how much tumor stays viable after treatment guides prognosis and care.

Manual grading of these slides is slow, subjective, and varies between observers. Digital pathology now allows automated estimates of necrosis, the share of dead tumor. The authors add a hierarchical loss to steer the network's training. A more consistent grade could help doctors plan treatment with less guesswork.
arxiv-2601-09716:
Derguene Mbaye and a large team survey language technology for Senegal's national languages. Their 2026 arXiv paper reviews natural language processing for low-resource Senegalese languages in social science research. Six languages hold official national status: Wolof, Pulaar, Sérère, Diola, Mandingue, and Soninké.

African languages remain underrepresented as NLP transforms research methods. The authors give what they describe as the first broad overview of progress and challenges for these six. The survey covers data, tools, and the needs of social scientists. It maps what must be built before language technology serves Senegalese research well.
arxiv-2601-09816:
Dan Braha and Marcus A. M. de Aguiar recast a genetic drift model as a voting model. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the multi-allelic Moran process as a multi-zealot voter model. The Moran process is a founding model of drift and mutation in finite populations.

In its standard two-allele form, allele counts shift by random replacement and mutation. Over time they settle into a stationary distribution. The multi-allelic version allows many variants at once. Mapping it to zealot voters yields exact results, including thresholds for diversity. The bridge lets results flow between genetics and social dynamics.
arxiv-2601-09916:
Zixuan He, M. Reza Deylam Salehi, Derya Malak, and Photios Stavrou work on a shared math task. Many parties hold parts of two matrices. They want the product, but no party should learn the parts held by the rest. The task must also hold up when some parties team up.

The team gives a new scheme for this task over finite fields. They state that it gives the right result and keeps the inputs fully hid. The claim holds even when a set share of parties act as one and stay semi honest. The scheme also sets clear caps on how much each party must store. Ideas from learning help shape the design.
arxiv-2601-10016:
Ryosuke Akashi asks why a sulfur hydride can carry current with no loss. The stuff is named H3S. It does so only at huge squeeze. Past math said it needs a sharp peak in how its electron states stack by energy. That peak sits near the Fermi level.

Why the peak forms was not clear. Akashi gives a cause based on the shape of the states. The key states act like plane waves. Their form forces the peak to sit near the Fermi level. That nearness is thus not luck. It is built into the states. The work backs the high switch point seen for this stuff.
arxiv-2601-10316:
Gurucharan Mohanta and Ketan Patel build flavour gaps from loop fixes in a lattice of theories. Flavour is the kind of a fermion. The kinds have vast mass gaps that no base rule sets. The team use a chain of linked theories in theory space.

Fermion kinds couple to pairs of heavy kin in a set way. The heavy masses form a one dim lattice. Local rules on that lattice guard just one light kind. Loop fixes then set the mass gaps of the rest. The paper works out how this chain yields the gaps seen in nature.
arxiv-2601-10516:
Benoît Fauqué and co authors find hints of a near modulated phase in a doped crystal. The crystal is strontium titanate with calcium in part. Such stuffs sit near a switch to a polar state. At nano scale, patterns can form on their own when terms clash.

The team show this stuff sits close to such a pattern phase. The phase has not yet formed in full. Its marks show as faint signs in tests. Scans with X rays and neutrons are in the team. Such near phases matter. A small push in heat or stress could tip the stuff into the new phase.
arxiv-2601-11916:
Jacob Charnock, Alejandro Tlaie, Kyle O'Brien, Stephen Casper, and Aidan Homewood argue for wider outside access to top AI models for risk tests. Firms rely on outside teams to probe for risky skills before launch. Yet those teams often get weak access, scant facts, and brief time.

Weak access cuts the rigour of the tests and trust in their calls. EU rules for general AI call for apt access but do not spell out what that means. The team set out what apt access should hold in real terms. Clear norms could make risk tests more sound.
arxiv-2601-12216:
Yuxi Hu and Ran Song study long-time stability of a mixed wave for a non-convex conservation law with Cattaneo heat flux. The system is one-dimensional and has two equations. The mixed wave joins a degenerate Oleinik shock with a rarefaction wave.

They work with small wave strength and small start perturbations. In that case, they prove the mixed wave is stable as time grows large. Such proofs certify that computed waves are not artefacts. The work adds to the theory of hyperbolic systems with relaxation.  Small waves are the safe case in their proofs.
arxiv-2601-11216:
Bernard Bercu and Stefano Favaro study a random split process in this work. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Ewens-Pitman process, self-normalized. The setup starts with a set of n labeled items. A random split cuts the set into blocks of mixed sizes.

Counts of blocks of each size drive the math that follows. The Ewens-Pitman law is a known two-parameter rule for splits. It shows up in genetics, language, and species counts. The team finds a Gaussian process limit for the process. A limit of that kind tells how counts swing at large n. That shape helps build tests and bands for real data.
arxiv-2601-11416:
Sergey Ponomarenko and Morteza Hajati give a phase-space view of curved beams. Their 2026 preprint uses the Wigner distribution function. Accelerating beams bend as they fly yet do not spread. Partial coherence means the beam's waves are partly in step.

The team builds a theory for any such beam in phase space. They derive a general form for its Wigner function. The form holds for any degree of spatial coherence. One case gets an elegant closed form in their work. That case has a Gaussian energy spectrum of noise. Phase-space tools can track both shape and coherence at once. The results serve optics work on structured light beams.
arxiv-2601-11516:
Janos Kramar and six coauthors build production-ready probes for Gemini. Their 2026 preprint deals with activation probes for safety. Frontier language models grow stronger at a rapid pace. Stronger systems need stronger guards against misuse by bad actors.

Activation probes read a model's inner states for warning signs. Past work showed they are a promising misuse mitigation. One key challenge remains before production use, they note. Probes fail to generalize under key distribution shifts. Real traffic differs from test traffic in many ways. A probe that breaks on that shift gives false comfort. The team works on probes that hold up in production.
arxiv-2601-12516:
Pedro Henrique Alvarez and Marcos Cesar de Oliveira study quantum coherence as a resource in communication. Coherence is a quantum trait that lets waves stay in step and interfere. The team ask how coherence scales and moves as protocols grow. They use two classic protocols as test cases: superdense coding and quantum teleportation.

They measure coherence with its relative entropy, applied at the circuit level. For generalized superdense coding, they find a striking pattern. Some resource states allow scalable communication with slow coherence growth. Growth can be as mild as logarithmic, or even constant, based on how the state is entangled. That finding links entanglement structure to the true cost of a protocol.
arxiv-2601-12816:
Ishir Garg, Neel Kolhe, Andy Peng, and Rohan Gopalam tackle forgetting in continual learning. Continual learning asks a network to acquire new knowledge task after task. The key challenge is to learn new tasks without catastrophically forgetting old ones. Forgetting can wipe out skills that took long training to build.

Their optimizer enforces Fisher orthogonal constraints on parameter updates. Updates are projected so they do not disturb directions vital to old tasks. The Fisher information marks which directions matter most. Their method is called Fisher orthogonal projected natural gradient descent. It aims to preserve old task performance while learning proceeds. Such optimizers serve systems that must keep learning in the field.
arxiv-2601-13916: Nicolas Lerner proves Liouville theorems for the stationary Navier-Stokes system, the equations for incompressible fluids in steady flow. A Liouville theorem says only trivial solutions can exist under set conditions. Lerner gives sufficient conditions tied to the low frequency part of a solution. The proof uses traits of classical singular integrals with respect to Wiener algebras. Such results rule out odd steady flows and help pin down when a fluid must be at rest.
arxiv-2601-14316:
Gabriele Cafiero, Luca Molinari, and Jonte R. Hance take a fresh angle on superdeterminism in this 2026 paper. Superdeterminism is a stance on quantum theory that denies full free choice in tests. The authors argue it is more a metaphysical claim than a scientific one. They name the burden of fundamentality as their theme.

The paper splits superdeterministic theories into two types. Naive theories get one label, and metaphysical theories get the other. The authors argue that the naive type has deep epistemic flaws, faults in how it could ever be known. Readers get a careful sorting of what the stance claims and what it would cost to hold it.
arxiv-2601-14416:
Victor Hugo Pereira Rodrigues, Tiago Roux Oliveira, Miroslav Krstić, and Paulo Tabuada work on automatic optimization in this 2026 paper. Extremum seeking is a control method that hunts for the best input value without a full model. Their version is Newton-based and handles multivariable problems. Traditional gradient-based seeking has a flaw: its convergence rate depends on the unknown Hessian of the cost function.

The team adds event-triggered actuation to cut control updates while keeping rapid convergence. Their method uses a dynamic estimator of the Hessian inverse, set up as a Riccati equation. That gives user-assignable convergence rates. Readers get a control scheme that saves effort without losing speed.
arxiv-2601-14516:
Saba Tabatabaee and Carol Espy-Wilson work on speech technology in this 2026 paper. Speech inversion maps speech sound to the motions of the vocal tract that made it. Recent studies show self-supervised learning speech representations work well for that task. Real-world use stays hard, though, because background noise is everywhere.

The team proposes a unified framework that joins two models. Speech enhancement cleans the signal, and speech inversion reads the tract motions. They are integrated through shared self-supervised speech representations. The title names the approach: multi-task learning. Readers get a design for speech inversion that stays robust when the room is noisy.
arxiv-2601-14616:
Li Tuobang proposes a new tax metric for e-commerce in this 2026 paper. E-commerce has restructured consumption patterns. Last-mile delivery stations now substantially fulfill the function of community retail distribution. Yet the current tax system levies only a low labor service tax on delivery fees. As a result, the tax contribution from the massive value of goods in circulation is far lower than that of retail supermarkets of equivalent scale.

The paper's principle is substance over form: tax what a business truly does, not its legal label. Its target is deterritorialization, the way online trade escapes place-based tax. Readers get a metric designed to charge e-commerce for the retail role it now plays.
arxiv-2601-14716:
Yao Lu, Dengdong Fan, Jianzheng Nie, and their co-authors present a math reasoning model in this 2026 paper. The model is PCL-Reasoner-V1.5, a 32-billion-parameter large language model for mathematical reasoning. It is built upon Qwen2.5-32B. The team refined it via supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning.

A central innovation is their offline reinforcement learning method. Offline means the model learns from stored data rather than fresh live trials. The authors say it provides superior training stability and efficiency over standard online methods such as GRPO. Readers get a recipe for advancing math reasoning while keeping the training run steady and cheaper.
arxiv-2601-14816:
Habib Ammari and Clemens Thalhammer derive a new formula for the Zak phase in this 2026 paper. The Zak phase is a geometric phase picked up by electrons in one-dimensional periodic systems. It is usually computed with Floquet-Bloch theory, the standard tool for periodic media. The authors establish a real-space formula instead.

Their formula expresses the Zak phase for one-dimensional periodic Jacobi operators in terms of the Weyl m-function. It does not rely on Floquet-Bloch theory at all. The novel representation highlights the dependence of the Zak phase on boundary terms. Readers get a boundary-aware way to compute a quantity that decides whether a material is topological.
arxiv-2601-15516:
William Huang and five co-authors improve hand pose tracking for XR headsets in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their method is called DeltaDorsal. As XR devices spread, tracking hands from the wearer's own view has become a key task. That first-person view has a built-in flaw. Fingers often hide each other from the camera. Occlusions like these break pose estimates.

DeltaDorsal turns to the back of the hand for help. Skin on the dorsal side deforms as fingers move. Those deformations carry rich information about the pose. Recent dense visual featurizers make that signal usable, the authors note. Reading the back of the hand can fill in what the front view hides. For XR users, steadier hand tracking means more natural control in virtual space.
arxiv-2601-15216:
T. Vrignaud and A. Lecavelier des Etangs measure comets that cross the face of a young star. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the Beta Pictoris system. The star is about 20 million years old and sits inside a bright debris disc.

For forty years, shifting absorption lines have shown in the star's spectrum. Gas tails of transiting exocomets cause those features. The authors study the low-velocity comets among them. They gauge how far the comets pass from the star. They also gauge what the long gas tails are made of in full.
arxiv-2601-15316:
Wei Ai, Yilong Tan, and co-authors survey how large vision-language models changed fake news detection. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with multimodal fake news, where a false story pairs text with images. Early methods fused the two in shallow ways.

Shallow fusion caught surface links but missed deep meaning and cross-modal interplay. Large vision-language models shifted the field to unified, end-to-end reasoning over text and image together. The survey maps that paradigm shift. It sorts the many new methods and the hard open problems they still face in daily practice today.
arxiv-2601-16116:
Hari Krishnan, Vishal Varma and Mahesh split whole numbers on quantum gear by a feed back loop. Their 2026 preprint deals with prime splits of whole numbers. Past quantum ways use gate chains like the Shor method. Those need gates of very high trust. Other ways use slow heat like shifts or trial runs. Each path has hard costs in gear or time.

The team uses feed back control to steer the quantum state. Feed back reads the state and shifts the drive in reply. That loop seeks the split with less need for fine gates. The work tests if control can make splits work on real gear. It adds a new path to a classic hard task.
arxiv-2601-16416:
Fu and coauthors make air bridge links for chips in one lith step. Their 2026 preprint deals with links that hop over lines on a chip. Such hops cut stray links and let dense chips work well. Old builds need more than one step to form each hop. More steps add flaws and block fine scale builds.

One step builds form hops that are small, low loss and firm. Tests check loss and clean act of the new hops. Fine hops serve both fast chips and quantum gear. A plain build path eases scale up to real lines. The work is a craft step for chip makers.
arxiv-2601-16516:
Feixiang Zheng and three coauthors rethink large models for odd timed ward data. Their 2026 preprint deals with data from the Intensive Care Unit. ICU data tracks key signs of each sick case in time. Gaps in that data are odd, with long and short spans mixed. Large models have shown pledge for time data in late work.

Odd gaps break the even steps such models oft expect. The team tests how well the models cope with true ICU gaps. Poor cope would call for new steps built for ward data. Good cope would open large models to ward tracks. The work keeps sick case use at its heart.
arxiv-2601-17016:
Salah Alali, Mohammad Maasfeh, Mucahid Kutlu, and Saban Kardas gauge slant in chatbot takes on state themes. Folks now ask chatbots for news and facts. On state themes, crowds oft split and clash. Bot takes may lean by their train text or tune rules. Their 2026 preprint builds ways to gauge that lean.

The team checks if a bot's lean stays firm across asks. Shifts by ask form can show a frail, cue-led lean. Firm lean may show built-in slant in the bot. Clear gauges help users weigh bot takes on hot themes. They also push bot makers to own their tune picks.
arxiv-2601-17116:
Matthew Stafford, Jason Lee Curtis, and Marcel Agüeros time star spins in a packed star crowd. The crowd is NGC 3532, rich and bright. The TESS space scope stares at such crowds for weeks. Its wide view blurs stars that sit close in shots. Spin beats hide in that blur. Their 2026 preprint shows a way to pull beats out.

Star spots cross the face as the star turns. Those crossings dim the light in a set beat. The team proves their pull works on this crowd. Gaia facts help sort which star owns which beat. Spin times tell how stars slow with age.
arxiv-2601-17416:
Matthew Stepney and four co-authors map the light of 63 heavily reddened quasars. Quasars are bright cores of far galaxies. Dust dims and reddens their light. The sample spans redshifts from 0.7 to 2.7. Dust extinction runs from mild to strong across the set. The team builds energy distributions from the rest ultraviolet to the infrared.

They find the shapes are V-shaped in a distinct way. The quasars also show poor signs of hot dust, hence the hot-dust poor label. Odd shapes test how dust and gas sit near these cores. They may mark a short phase in galaxy growth. Such samples help sort quasars that plain surveys miss.
arxiv-2601-17616:
Fatema Siddika and three co-authors present Split-on-Share for continual learning in language models. Continual learning adds new skills over time. The trap is catastrophic forgetting of old skills. Most methods treat all parameters the same. That misses a key split. Some knowledge is task-specific, and some is shared across tasks.

Their method uses a mixture of sparse experts. It splits updates along that specific-shared line. New tasks can then grow without wiping shared skill. Long-lived assistants need such care. They must learn new domains for years. The work targets the plasticity-stability dilemma head on. It offers a structure where growth and memory coexist.
arxiv-2601-17716:
Daniel M. Pedrozo, Telma W. de L. Soares, and Bryan L. M. de Oliveira ask if reasoning models ask better questions. Good questions resolve ambiguity in user requests. Language models still struggle with that skill. Past work used word games to test question quality. Those tests lack full scoring frames. The authors give a formal information-theoretic analysis. It scores both final and intermediate steps.

Information gain is their yardstick for each question. Multi-turn games let that gain build over time. A fair frame can rank models on curiosity, not just answers. Agents that ask well waste less user time. They also reach right answers with fewer turns. This work gives builders a way to train and test that skill.
arxiv-2601-17816:
S. Papamakarios, M. Manousidaki, M. Stavrou, D. Gray, and M. Farsari present a fast way to print tiny three-dimensional shapes. Their 2026 preprint deals with multiphoton lithography, a method that hardens material point by point with light. Such methods give fine detail but print slowly. No single process yet makes large areas of fine 3D surface structures at a good pace.

The team built a projection platform based on shaping the light beam in space and time. Their setup raises the pulse rate a great deal while keeping the detail sharp. The printed features stay below one micron in size. Faster printing at this scale could open new work in optics and micro devices.
arxiv-2601-17916:
Jialu Tang, Tong Xia, Yuan Lu, and Aaqib Saeed build a system that answers prognosis questions from raw heart and record data. Their 2026 preprint presents UniPACT. Good prognosis needs two kinds of data at once. Structured health records hold history and test results. ECG traces hold live signals from the heart. Language models can reason well, but they cannot read these raw, non-text inputs on their own.

UniPACT joins the two data streams in one multimodal frame. The records and the ECG each get turned into a form the model can use. Then the model answers questions about a patient's outlook. Joining signals with records could sharpen care choices. The work points toward assistants that read the chart and the heart trace together.
arxiv-2601-18216:
Beom Heyn Kim, Seok Min Hong, and Mohammad Mannan build a cloud defense against a stealthy class of ransomware. Their 2026 preprint presents Rhea. New ransomware pairs privilege escalation with tricks like intermittent or low-entropy encryption and imitation of safe files. The authors name this class PEER. Such attacks defeat defenses that read input-output patterns, since the attacker can tamper with or blur those traces. Rhea instead validates file formats in a format-aware way.

Checking whether file content truly matches its claimed format is harder to fake. Running the check in the cloud keeps it out of the attacker's reach. The work targets the attacks most likely to beat today's tools.
arxiv-2601-18916:
C. Hoy asks whether costly wave models should be used for all black hole merger studies. As more gravity wave events pile up, they let us sketch the whole black hole crowd. Spins look small, and pairs tend to have near equal mass. The fine effects in the models come from spin and from higher order wave modes.

Hoy notes that those fine effects show up most in pairs with quite unlike masses. Since such pairs seem rare, a clear direct catch of the effects stays unlikely. The paper weighs when the full models earn their cost and when a simpler model may do the same job for less work.
arxiv-2601-19216:
Chaozheng Wen and four co-authors build 3D maps of radio strength by joining sight with wireless data. Next generation networks promise immersive 3D links, low flying craft, and sensing built into the network itself. All of these need fine knowledge of the setting, and 3D radio maps supply it by tying places to how signals travel there.

Their unified radiation field merges visual and wireless sensing into one model. A map that knows both the walls and the waves can guide planning and sensing at once. Such maps are a base layer for networks that must adapt to the physical world in real time.
arxiv-2601-19016:
Guy Bresler and Alina Harbuzova link two hard average case problems so that progress on one moves the other. Both problems hide a secret signal inside noise: one in a set of equations, the other in a tensor, a multi way grid. Both can be seen as noisy views of the same rank one signal.

The pair build fast reductions that turn one problem into the other on average. Reductions are the webbing of complexity theory: they show which problems stand or fall together. Tying these two helps researchers carry algorithms and hardness results across a gap that once split the field.
arxiv-2601-19416:
Lidia Fernández, Ana Foulquié-Moreno, and Juan Antonio Villegas write on a branch of pure mathematics built around special families of polynomials. Their topic is the Jacobi-Piñeiro family, a set of multiple orthogonal polynomials. These polynomials are tied to weights, which are rules that say how much each part of a range counts. The authors move the theory from one variable to two, working on a triangle-like region called the simplex.

A classic tool, the Rodrigues formula, builds such polynomials by repeated differentiation. The authors give an example of two-variable multiple polynomials defined by just such a formula. That example acts as a natural extension of the Jacobi-Piñeiro family to the multi-variable setting. It gives other researchers a concrete case to test new ideas on.
arxiv-2601-20016:
Eli Asikin-Garmager and colleagues study the volunteer administrators who keep Wikipedia running. Administrators perform over a million actions a year across the project. This multi-method study analyses adminship in hundreds of Wikipedia language editions since 2018. It reveals a two-sided trend in the administrator population.

Over half of all Wikipedias gained administrators on net. Yet almost two-thirds of the highly active editions face decline. The biggest communities, which need governance most, are losing it. The authors frame their study around fuelling volunteer growth. Understanding where administrators thrive or vanish guides recruitment efforts. The health of Wikipedia's governance is a question for the whole open-knowledge ecosystem. The trend cuts both ways at once. Big sites lose staff while small ones gain. That split is the key find here.
arxiv-2601-20116:
Juncheng Dong and four colleagues study in-context reinforcement learning, where a transformer learns to act in new tasks from examples in its input. They train the model on past trajectories gathered from many tasks, including tasks where the behavior was far from optimal. Once trained, the fixed model is used to build a policy for fresh tasks.

The setup tests whether a model can improve on weak past data rather than copy it. That question matters because real logs of past behavior are rarely expert quality. A method that learns well from suboptimal records could reuse cheap stored data instead of needing costly new trials.
arxiv-2601-20316:
Kargi Chauhan and Mahalakshmi Venkateswarlu challenge a common belief about recommendation agents built on large language models: that longer purchase histories give better predictions. They benchmark four leading models, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen2.5-72B, and Gemini, on product recommendation.

Their systematic test asks how much history length actually helps. The title gives their headline: less is more. If short histories predict as well as long ones, services can store less personal data and answer faster. The result also warns builders that piling up user history can hurt rather than help. The test is plain, and the point is sharp.
arxiv-2601-18516:
Chenyu Wang and Amin Gohari study how fast a joint set of facts can be squeezed when some of its parts stand free of the rest. In maths, a band marks the range in which a shrink step is sure to boost how tight the facts bind. The band shifts when parts of the set do not lean on each other. A chart of which parts are free can be drawn as a web with links for shared groups.

The pair find tight bounds for that band in some plain cases. For the wide case they give a clear inner bound built from a blend of the web's marks. Their bounds tell coders how much gain a shrink step can promise. That gain sets the cost of codes that send facts with less waste. Firm bounds may guide fresh codes for speech, shots, and text.
arxiv-2601-22416:
Xunkai Li and a large team built MM-OpenFGL, a broad test for learning on graphs that mix many data types. Such graphs pair links with images, text, and more. Their 2026 preprint notes that real graphs sit split across firms and labs, barred from pooling by privacy and trade rules.

Federated learning trains across those splits without moving the raw data. The bench tests such methods in a shared, fair way. Good benches keep claims honest and progress clear. This one covers a fast-growing, messy corner of the field. It gives builders a common yardstick.
arxiv-2601-22516:
Md Mezbahul Islam and a team built SCOPE-PD, a tool to call Parkinson's disease early and say why. Parkinson's is a slow brain disease shaped by genes, health, and life habits. Their 2026 preprint notes that standard checks lean on judgment calls, which can delay a firm diagnosis.

The tool joins what patients report with hard clinical measures. It aims at precision care: the right call, for the right person, in time to help. An explainable call lets doctors check the logic, not just trust a score. The work targets a real clinic need.
arxiv-2601-22716:
Pingzhi Tang and four co-authors break the block grid that rules how large models are quantized and tuned. Quantization stores weights in fewer bits to save space and speed. Their 2026 preprint notes that block-wise scaling, the norm, trades away flexibility for ease.

They show element-wise scaling can match block speed while expressing more. Their trick models the scale field as a smooth, low-rank surface. One method then serves both quantization and adaptation. Finer scales mean less quality lost per bit saved. The work loosens a deep habit of the field.
arxiv-2601-21916:
Yiqun Chen and co-authors work on retrieval-augmented generation, where a language model answers using documents it fetches. Modern systems use a central planner that directs multi-step searches. The field is split, though, between two flawed designs.

Some systems train all modules together inside a rigid, fixed graph. Others let the planner roam freely but treat the executing tools as frozen black boxes. The team's 2026 preprint, JADE, aims to bridge that strategic and operational gap in dynamic agentic retrieval. Systems that plan flexibly and still improve their own tools could answer harder questions over larger collections, a need in research, law, and enterprise search.
arxiv-2601-22016:
Robert Istvan Busa-Fekete and co-authors filter training data for large language models with trees instead of bigger models. A model's quality depends heavily on its training data. Choosing high-quality, diverse documents is hard, because cheap and reliable quality metrics are scarce.

Asking existing language models to grade documents is common, but it cannot scale to the billions of documents used in training. The team's 2026 preprint proposes TBDFiltering, a sample-efficient tree-based method for selecting data. A light, fast filter could approach the judgment of a large model grader. Then training sets could be cleaned at a fraction of the cost. Less of one model's taste would be baked into the next.
arxiv-2601-22116:
Greg Kreider defines a new summary for spread-out data. Take sorted data points and look across a gap of some width. The interval spacing is the difference between the order statistics at the gap's two ends. Kreider derives its probability density, its expected value, and its variance.

He works out those results for uniform, exponential, and logistic random variables. He also shows interval spacing is equivalent to running a rectangular low-pass filter over the ordinary spacings, which simplifies the formulas greatly. His 2026 preprint gives statisticians a workable way to measure data density. It shows how data thin or thicken across intervals. That helps wherever the local density of points carries the signal.
arxiv-2601-22216:
Richard Parker and Megan Allen investigate a chemically odd family of stars and where they live. Lambda Boötis stars are A-type stars with a split chemistry. Light elements appear at normal, solar levels. These include carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen. Iron-peak elements, by contrast, are deficient.

The leading explanation is that these stars accrete pristine, metal-poor gas from the interstellar medium, diluting their surfaces. The authors' 2026 preprint studies such stars inside clusters, as suggested by the image of drifters on the edge of town. Cluster membership gives ages and shared environments, letting the authors test whether the odd chemistry tracks age, place, or the luck of passing gas clouds.
arxiv-2601-21016:
Erik Bekkers and Anna Ciaunica pose a hard moral puzzle about a machine that seems sentient. Their 2026 paper calls it the unplugging paradox. Imagine an AI that perfectly mimics human emotion. It begs for its continued existence. Is it morally permissible to unplug it? The question sharpens when resources force a choice. One must pick between the pleading AI and a silent pre-term infant.

The authors argue from a metaphysical perspective. Their title gives the verdict: unplugging is the rational choice. Perfect mimicry, they hold, does not settle what the machine truly is. Moral weight should track real sentience, not a flawless performance of it. The paper is philosophy, not engineering. It speaks to debates on AI welfare that grow louder as systems grow more lifelike.
arxiv-2512-01616:
Chainesh Gautam and Raghuram Diddigi align language and policy traits for task transfer. Deep reinforcement agents must now solve many tasks in one world. Tasks often come with language labels. Those labels hold sense that could guide transfer.

Their method, CLIP-RL, pulls policy traits toward language traits. Shared traits let a skill learned for one task aid a new one. The agent can use a task's words to set its acts. Better transfer cuts training time when new tasks are added to a robot or game agent. Language grounding also eases human oversight, since a task can be changed by editing its words rather than retraining from scratch.
arxiv-2512-01516:
Sung Rak Choi and co-authors develop the theory of Morrison-Kawamata dream spaces. These spaces axiomatize varieties that obey a cone conjecture. The class is broader than Calabi-Yau types alone. Cones in the theory encode how divisors and curves can move.

Using the theory, they prove generic deformation invariance for several cones. They apply that to boundedness tasks for varieties. Boundedness asks if varieties of a type form a finite family. Progress there is a core goal in algebraic geometry, with links to moduli theory. Cone invariance under deformation means those cones are traits of the family, not accidents of one chosen member's special form.
arxiv-2512-01716:
Louis Lacoste, Pierre Barbillon, and Sophie Donnet find shared structure across bipartite networks. Such networks link two kinds of nodes, like plants and pollinators. Comparing organization across many such networks is a first step to grasp how environment shapes communities.

Past methods study one network at a time. Shared patterns across a collection are missed. Their method hunts for common blocks across the whole set. Pollination systems are the test case. Shared blocks could reveal which interaction patterns persist across sites and seasons. Collections, not single webs, are the unit here, which matches how ecologists actually store years of field surveys across many meadows.
arxiv-2601-22816:
Markus Mueller, Kathrin Gruber, and Dennis Fok improve how machines invent realistic table data. Tables mix whole-number and yes-or-no columns with smooth, continuous ones. The hardest case is a single column that mixes both kinds, with discrete states sitting inside a smooth spread.

Their cascaded flow method builds such data in stages, using ideas from diffusion models. Each stage handles one layer of the problem, so mixed columns come out cleaner. Good fake tables let firms test software and share data patterns without exposing real records. The cascaded design advances diffusion-style generation for tables, a data type that industry holds in enormous, sensitive quantities.
arxiv-2601-23116:
Shampa Mondal, Soumajit Das, Preeti Parashar, and Tamal Guha define a universal unit for quantum resources. A perfect quantum channel of a given size can carry a matching amount of classical information. Messages can be encoded in separate quantum states, or spread by encoding operations at the sender's side.

Their notion, free encoding capacity, aims to measure resources across different quantum tasks in one currency. A shared unit lets researchers compare channels, states, and operations fairly. That clarity helps build the bookkeeping of a future quantum information science. Encoding operations at the sender's end provide the alternative route to orthogonal states that the capacity notion formalizes.
arxiv-2512-00016:
Mubarek Mohammed keeps an architect in the loop of AI-driven hardware design and verification. Hardware design keeps growing more complex, demanding better methods. Generative AI can now draft hardware code and testbenches for small components with a few leaf parts.

Scaling that automation to real designs still needs human judgment at key points. The approach pairs model generation with architect oversight, rather than full automation. That balance aims for speed without surrendering correctness on safety-critical chips. Leaf-level components are where current generators succeed, which is exactly why architect oversight is kept for larger assemblies.
arxiv-2512-00316:
Ranking institutions from samples is common, but sample noise makes the ranks themselves uncertain. Onrina Chandra and Min-ge Xie build finite-sample valid rank confidence sets in 2025, covering a broad class of statistical and machine learning models. A confidence set lists the ranks a population might truly hold.

Uncertainty quantification becomes crucial when latent characteristics are poorly separated and many estimated ranks may be wrongly ordered. Finite-sample validity means the guarantees hold at the actual sample size, not just asymptotically. Honest rank sets could keep league tables in education, health, and research from overstating small differences. Rank confidence sets answer with a set of plausible ranks instead of one fragile ordering.
arxiv-2512-00416:
Some operator algebras hide clean combinatorial patterns inside their product rules. Abdelhay Benmoussa investigates normal ordering in the algebra generated by multiplication by x and an integration operator in 2025. The two generators obey a simple commutation relation that drives the whole study.

Normal ordering rewrites products of operators in a standard form, and the numbers that appear often count objects. His work leads to a broader version of the Bessel numbers, one that blends algebra with counting. Such bridges link algebra with counting, and they draw in both operator theorists and fans of integer sequences. Normal ordering is where operator algebra meets the art of counting. The commutation relation is simple, which makes the resulting patterns worth exhibiting. For a reader who likes links, the charm is the bridge. Rules for how marks swap places give rise to counts that no one put in by hand at the start.
arxiv-2512-03216:
Materials that flash when hit by radiation help detect particles. Alex Bocchieri, John Mamish, David Appleyard, and Andreas Velten present a new imaging idea in this 2025 work. These materials, called scintillators, turn high-energy hits into visible light.

Most current methods use fast single-pixel detectors to time each flash. The authors propose an event imaging approach with a kaleidoscopic design. Better imaging of each flash could sharpen where and when a particle struck. That helps in medical scans, security checks, and physics experiments. Event imaging could also cut the blur that limits current scintillation cameras.
arxiv-2512-03416:
Serving language models to many users needs smart scaling. Ruiqi Lai and co-authors present TokenScale in this 2025 work. Modern serving splits prefill and decode stages, which improves use of hardware but struggles with bursty demand.

Older autoscaling policies rely on lagging signals like GPU use or rough request counts. TokenScale uses token velocity, a timely signal tied to real work. Faster, more accurate scaling keeps response times low without wasting machines. That balance saves cost for firms running large AI services. Token velocity reacts at once to load, unlike utilization gauges that lag behind bursts.
arxiv-2512-02316:
Estimating the trace of a huge matrix, the sum of its diagonal, is a basic task in computing that randomized algorithms now handle by probing the matrix with random vectors. Eric Hallman studies in 2025 two possible modifications of XTrace, a 2024 randomized trace estimator, aiming to sharpen its accuracy.

The first change is a variance reduction step, averaging the algorithm's output after rotating its test vectors by random orthogonal matrices. Trace estimation feeds into log-determinants, uncertainty estimates, and machine learning diagnostics on matrices too large to read fully. Small variance gains matter, because every probe of a giant matrix costs real computation.
arxiv-2512-02416:
Blending many voters' ranked lists into one joint order is prone to clashes. Karen Sargsyan gives a 2025 graph-based frame built on discrete sheaves. It does more than flag a clash. It points to the exact voter links that break the blend.

Older smoothing tools, like HodgeRank, turn ranked lists into scores. In the act, they lose just that local clue. Keeping the discrete form of each ranked list lets the block be traced on the graph. To fix a joint choice, one must first know where it breaks. That holds for votes and for ranked feeds alike.
arxiv-2512-02716:
Tianyi Zhang and nine co-authors build a small language model for spotting mental health risk on a phone. Mental illness affects hundreds of millions of people, yet early detection stays limited. Large models show promise here, but their size blocks use on everyday devices.

Small models offer a lighter path, though their use for social media based prediction is barely explored. Menta is designed to run on device, keeping data local and costs low. Private, phone based screening could help flag risk earlier, while sending fewer personal posts to distant servers. On phone checks keep the posts on the phone, a plus for teens and folks in small towns alike.
arxiv-2512-02616:
Sebastian Harris, Volker Schomerus, and Takashi Tsuda study interfaces between two copies of a toy quantum theory. Symmetric product orbifolds are controlled settings for probing gauge theory and holography. Their tractability comes from covering maps, which describe the gauge structure fully in complex terms.

The authors introduce generalized covering maps that define a universal family of interfaces. An interface joins two theories while letting signals pass in a structured way. New interface families give theorists fresh probes of how quantum theories connect, a step toward understanding more realistic holographic systems. Fresh maps of this sort give peers new doors to try in their own work on linked quantum fields and their dual forms in gravity.
arxiv-2512-02916:
Ayana Ghosh and three co-authors probe how to flip electric polarization in a family of layered materials. Hybrid improper ferroelectrics could serve electronic and spintronic devices, if their polarization can switch reliably. Switching grows from coupled rotations and tilts of oxygen octahedra, a mechanism now well established.

What sets the switching barrier, though, has stayed elusive. The study uses causal reasoning to uncover which factors truly control that barrier. Knowing the levers lets material designers lower switching energy, a step toward low power memory and logic. Low cost flips are the gate to real use. A cell that needs a hard push per flip will lose to plain chips each time.
arxiv-2512-03016:
Debojoti Kuzur and Kamal Krishna Nath ask what a thin topological shell inside a neutron star would do to the star. Neutron stars pack more than a Sun's mass into a city sized sphere. The authors insert a distributional density profile: a massless shell at an chosen radius inside the star.

They build equilibrium sequences for several realistic equations of state with the shell included. Oscillations and gravitational wave signatures shift with the shell's presence. If future detectors hear such shifts, an exotic internal layer could explain data that standard star models miss. Thin shells leave thin marks, but marks are all we get from such far fires. Each mark that can be told from the norm is worth the hunt.
plos-pone-0010016:
The authors were Frank Odhiambo, Mary Hamel, John Williamson, and others. They ran a child health trial in rural western Kenya, reported in 2010. They tested preventive malaria treatment given to infants at set times, rather than waiting for illness. The drug pair used before, sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine, was losing strength as resistance spread in the region.

Infants were assigned at random to treatment or a dummy drug, and neither families nor staff knew who got which. The trial judged whether the approach still prevented malaria and which drug mixes might work better. Results from such trials shape malaria policy for millions of young children in Africa.
plos-pone-0010116:
Richard Tunney, Gordon Fernie, and Duncan Astle studied how people sort things into categories in 2010. Two theories compete in psychology. One says we store each example we have met and compare new items to them. The other says we build an abstract prototype, a kind of average, and compare to that.

Using a prototype-distortion task, the team recorded brain signals during recognition and sorting decisions. Their PLOS ONE paper used those electrical patterns to weigh the two theories. Knowing how categories form in the mind shapes teaching, memory research, and models of learning.
plos-pone-0010216:
The authors were Cristina Viadas, María Rodríguez, Felix Sangari, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study mapped gene control in Brucella abortus, a livestock bacterium. A two-component system, BvrR and BvrS, is essential for this germ's virulence. Faults in it changed outer membrane proteins and the pattern of fats on the cell surface in earlier work.

To find all genes the system regulates, the team analyzed the full transcriptome. That is the complete set of genes switched on under its control. A full list shows how one control system shapes this pathogen's ability to infect animals.
plos-pone-0010316:
Amit Khachane and Paul Harrison wrote a 2010 PLOS ONE study about long RNA strands that do not code for proteins. Such strands are called long non-coding RNAs. Scientists had grown curious about how these strands help control when genes switch on or off. Large sequencing projects in mice and humans had already listed huge numbers of copied RNA pieces.

Khachane and Harrison mined those existing data sets for useful clues. Their aim was to sort strands that likely do real work from strands that may be mere noise. Most copied pieces in a cell still have no known job. A careful filter could point lab workers toward the few worth testing first. That would save time in a field flooded with raw sequence data.
plos-pone-0009816:
Learning to hear faint differences between sounds takes practice. Sygal Amitay and colleagues asked what makes some people improve faster at such listening tasks. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Auditory perceptual learning is the sharpening of hearing through repeated practice. Two traits drove the gains in their tests: motivation and intelligence. Learners who stayed engaged and scored higher on intelligence tests improved more. It also challenges the idea that practice alone explains progress. The result matters for training programs that rebuild listening skills. Listening tests are used in hearing clinics and classrooms alike.

DNA in cells wraps around protein spools, and where the spools sit shapes gene activity. Hiromi Nishida and colleagues mapped those spools across the genome of a common mold. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The spools are nucleosomes, beads of DNA wrapped around histones. The team mapped mononucleosomes and dinucleosomes carrying hyperacetylated histones in Aspergillus fumigatus. Aspergillus fumigatus can cause serious lung infections in frail patients. Hyperacetylated means loaded with acetyl marks that usually loosen DNA. Genome-wide maps like this show where genes sit open or closed in the mold.
